**Neither answer is correct.** The sum is at least 341, so it is not 336 or 80.

**Structural facts.** Every row and column has exactly n entries, so every r_i and c_j has exactly n divisors. The entry r_i must sit in a column whose c-value is a multiple of r_i with n divisors, so c-values are exactly the r-values, one per column. Put r_i on the diagonal. Then any proper divisor d of r_i must also divide some other r_l, since d cannot sit on the diagonal. Comparing exponents, if r has a prime q with exponent e, then some other r_l has exponent e−1 at q and at least the same exponents elsewhere, with the same divisor count. This forces e(e+1) | n for every exponent e that occurs.

**Consequences.**
- For any prime p, some exponent e has p | (e+1), so e ≥ p−1 and n ≥ p(p−1). Hence S(7) ≥ 42, S(11) ≥ 110, S(13) ≥ 156.
- B's values S(7)=14, S(11)=22, S(13)=26 violate this bound, so 80 is wrong.
- S(3)=6 holds. A's 6×6 table is valid (B's misreading of column 4 is wrong), and n=3 is impossible, since r_i would be q_i^2 and the witness for q_i fails.
- For p=5, the multiples of 5 up to 20 are 5, 10, 15, 20. Exponents must satisfy e(e+1) | n, which gives:
  - n=5 and n=10 fail, since no exponent e with 5 | (e+1) satisfies e(e+1) | n.
  - n=15 fails for the same reason.
  - n=20 forces every r to have shape x⁴yz. For the prime x, the witness needs (f_y+1)(f_z+1)·(other factors) = 5 with f_y, f_z ≥ 1. That is impossible, so n=20 fails.
- So S(5) ≥ 25, and A's claim S(5)=20 is false.

**Bound on the sum.** Using S(2)=2, S(3)=6, S(5) ≥ 25, S(7) ≥ 42, S(11) ≥ 110, S(13) ≥ 156, the sum is at least 341. That rules out both 336 and 80. I did not determine the exact values of S(5), S(7), S(11), S(13).

DECISION: NEITHER
